mcqs.question: Why can't a key-value store answer a query like "all users who signed up this week"?
options: The store treats values as opaque and can only look them up by their key, with no visibility into their contents
Key-value stores don't support timestamps as data
That query requires more memory than key-value stores can allocate
Key-value stores can only hold string values, not structured user data
mcqs.explanation: A key-value store's entire model is opaque values addressed by key — it has no way to filter on a field inside the value without a secondary index or a separate system. Timestamps can be stored fine as data; the limitation is about queryability, not memory or value type.

mcqs.question: Why are column-family stores like Cassandra well suited to high-write, time-ordered data such as sensor readings?
options: They store data purely in memory, so writes never touch disk
Appending a new column for a row is a cheap, sequential write rather than an update to a fixed-width row
They automatically convert writes into batched SQL transactions
They replicate every write to every node before acknowledging it
mcqs.explanation: Column-family storage groups a row's columns together and appends new ones cheaply and sequentially, which is what makes high write throughput possible. They aren't purely in-memory, don't use SQL transactions internally, and don't require full replication before acknowledging a write.

mcqs.question: A team needs to detect fraud rings by finding accounts connected through shared devices, addresses, and payment methods several hops apart. Which model fits best?
options: Key-value store, keyed by account ID
Column-family store, keyed by account ID
Graph database, modeling accounts and shared attributes as connected nodes
Document store, with each account as a separate document
mcqs.explanation: Multi-hop relationship traversal is exactly what graph databases are built for — the query is about the connections themselves, not a lookup by a single key. Key-value, column-family, and document models can all store the same facts but make multi-hop traversal expensive or awkward.

mcqs.question: A document store schema stores users and orders as separate collections linked by `userId`, requiring a separate fetch for every order after fetching a user. What's the better default?
options: Switch to a graph database instead
Keep the reference pattern but cache every order in memory
Add a relational database alongside the document store just for orders
Embed data that's read together and rarely updated independently, like an order's line items inside the order document
mcqs.explanation: Document stores favor embedding data that's read together and changes together, avoiding the extra round trips a reference pattern forces. A graph database or a second relational database adds unneeded complexity for this shape of data, and caching papers over the round-trip cost without fixing the underlying model mismatch.
